name: Thorn scrub
notes: Semi-arid thorny woodland/scrub: small spiny legumes and succulents on dry, often thin soils with a sparse grass layer. Drawn on the Caatinga (Brazil), Chaco (Argentina/Paraguay), Tamaulipan thornscrub (Mexico/Texas), Somali-Masai Acacia-Commiphora bushland and Madagascar spiny thicket.

canopy.name: Honey mesquite
canopy.origin: SW United States and northern Mexico
canopy.source: Prosopis glandulosa, Tamaulipan thornscrub/Chihuahuan Desert (Mexico, SW USA), thorny deciduous legume 5-12 m — Wikipedia / USDA Plants

traits.native_range: Prosopis glandulosa, Tamaulipan thornscrub/Chihuahuan Desert (Mexico, SW USA), thorny deciduous legume 5-12 m — Wikipedi
traits.trunk: short twisted trunk, heavy low limbs, wind-shaped
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

canopy.silhouette: low wide feathery crown on crooked trunk

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two thick oblong cotyledons, a first once-pinnate leaf, then bright green, feathery bipinnate leaves with a few pairs of long leaflets and paired spines at the nodes of a zigzag stem. The taproot races ahead and a bud zone at the stem base resprouts if the top is killed, so young plants become low, thorny, multi-stemmed bushes; suppressed plants decades old can look like seedlings.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Prosopis glandulosa (scarified seed germinates in ~7 h at 33 C; best emergence from 0.5-1.5 cm; seed by age 3; 27-yr-old plants 0.2-1.5 m in an exclosure; trees 6-12 m; max ages 110-217 yr, most under 100); ICRAF Agroforestree (3-9 m; first fruit at 3-4 yr).

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS P. glandulosa (spring racemes with the leaves; bee pollinated, 160+ bee species; pods 10-20 cm, ~12 seeds, mature in 2-3 months, fall by late summer; 97-131 pods/tree in one study); ICRAF (racemes 5-14 cm; pods 8-30 cm, straw-yellow or violet-tinged). Flowers per raceme, fruit set and decay estimated.

canopy.name: Texas ebony
canopy.source: Ebenopsis ebano, Texas ebony, thorny evergreen shrub/small tree of Tamaulipan thornscrub, 3-8 m — Wikipedia

traits.native_range: Ebenopsis ebano, Texas ebony, thorny evergreen shrub/small tree of Tamaulipan thornscrub, 3-8 m — Wikipedia
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

growth.juvenile_note: Hard seeds germinate after scarification; epigeal, then small bipinnate leaves with a few pairs of tiny, dark, rounded leaflets. The seedling is a bushy, zigzag-branched shrub armed with paired spines at each node, often several stems from the base; it slowly forms a dense, dark-green, rounded evergreen crown and can be raised as a small single-trunked tree.
growth.source: Wikipedia Ebenopsis ebano (7.6-9.1 m, crown 1.8-4.6 m; fragrant flowers; seedpods host bean weevils; dry forest and matorral of S Texas and NE Mexico, 20-27 C, ~900 mm rain). Growth rate, fruiting age, lifespan and germination estimated from Texas native-plant horticulture.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (fragrant flowers; seedpods attacked by bean weevils). Creamy catkin-like spikes in early summer after rains, thick woody dark pods 10-15 cm that hang on through winter, and seeds eaten green-boiled or roasted as a coffee substitute are from Texas native-plant references; set, crop and decay estimated.

canopy.name: Huisache
canopy.source: Vachellia farnesiana (Acacia farnesiana), huisache or sweet acacia: a thorny shrub or small tree 3-8 m with paired straight white spines, feathery bipinnate leaves and fragrant golden pompom flowers in late winter; native in the Tamaulipan thornscrub of south Texas and NE Mexico and through tropical America, naturalised widely elsewhere — Kew POWO / Flora of North America / USDA FEIS

leaf.note: 2-8 pairs of pinnae with tiny narrow leaflets, often clustered at the nodes beside paired straight white spines

canopy.silhouette: low flat-topped thorny tree, gold pompoms in late winter

growth.juvenile_note: Hard seeds sprout after passing through cattle or being scarified, usually after rain. The seedling is a thin zig-zag stem with paired white spines and small feathery leaves; it grows fast in open pasture, branching low into a many-stemmed shrub or a short-trunked small tree with a flat, spreading crown, and resprouts from the base when cut or burned.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Acacia farnesiana (shrub or tree to ~9 m; seeds hard-coated, germinate after scarification; sprouts from the root crown after top-kill; fruits within a few years; increases on grazed rangeland in south Texas). Height curve and lifespan estimated.

fruiting.source: Flora of North America and USDA FEIS Vachellia farnesiana (very fragrant golden ball-shaped heads 1-1.5 cm, 2-5 per node, Feb-Mar in south Texas, bee-pollinated; thick, nearly cylindrical dark brown to black pods 4-8 cm that stay closed and hang on the tree). Set and crop estimated.

bark.notes: grey-brown bark, smooth on young stems and shallowly fissured on old trunks; paired straight white spines at each node

leaf.notes: feathery bipinnate leaves of tiny narrow leaflets

flower.form: fragrant golden pompom flower heads crowding the twigs in late winter

fruit.form: thick dark brown to black cylindrical pods that stay on the tree

appearance.silhouette: flat-topped thorny tree glowing gold above the brush in late winter
appearance.refs: Kew POWO; Flora of North America vol. 11; USDA FEIS

canopy.name: Mexican palo verde
canopy.source: Parkinsonia aculeata, Fabaceae: retama or Jerusalem thorn, a green-barked thorny small tree 3-8 m with long wispy leaves and yellow flowers, native from south Texas and the Tamaulipan thornscrub through Mexico to the Chaco and the Caatinga — Kew POWO / Flora of North America / Flora del Paraguay

leaf.note: a short spiny midrib carries 1-3 pairs of long flat green pinnae with tiny leaflets that drop in drought

canopy.silhouette: wispy green-barked tree with drooping leaves

growth.juvenile_note: Hard seeds sprout after scarification or a wet season. The seedling is a slender green zig-zag stem with paired spines and long thread-like leaves; it grows fast and flowers in a few years, becoming a low, wide, open tree whose green bark keeps photosynthesising when the tiny leaflets fall in drought.
growth.source: Kew POWO and Flora of North America Parkinsonia aculeata (shrub or tree to 10 m, green bark, pinnae 20-40 cm with 25-60 tiny leaflets, flowers spring-summer); USDA plant guide (fast-growing, flowers from 3 yr, short-lived). Lifespan estimated.

fruiting.source: Flora of North America Parkinsonia aculeata (fragrant yellow flowers 2 cm in loose racemes, the upper petal red-spotted, bee-pollinated, spring to summer and after rain; pods 5-15 cm constricted between the seeds). Set and crop estimated.

bark.notes: smooth yellow-green bark on trunk and branches, brown and rough only at the base; paired thorns

leaf.notes: long flat green ribbon-like pinnae lined with tiny leaflets that fall in drought

flower.form: loose sprays of bright yellow five-petalled flowers, one petal red-spotted

fruit.form: slender brown pods pinched between the seeds

appearance.seasonal: leaflets drop in drought; yellow bloom spring and after rain
appearance.silhouette: green-barked tree with a lacy drooping crown in thornscrub
appearance.refs: Kew POWO; Flora of North America vol. 11; USDA plant guide

canopy.name: Camel thorn

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal, with two thick oval cotyledons and grey-green feathery bipinnate leaves on a zigzag stem armed with pairs of large, swollen-based, white spines. The seedling pours its effort into a taproot that heads down toward groundwater (in old trees it may reach tens of metres) while the shoot grows slowly, so young plants are sparse, very spiny, grey-green bushes for years.
growth.source: SANBI PlantZAfrica (Vachellia erioloba): 2 m shrub to 16 m tree, slow-growing, starts flowering at about 10 years, seeds take 4-6 weeks to germinate after a boiling-water soak, taproot can reach 60 m; ICRAF Agroforestree: flowers at about 10 yr, regular pod crops by 20 yr, crown to 18 m. Height curve and lifespan estimated.

canopy.source: Kalahari. Kew POWO (African acacias are now Vachellia/Senegalia; Acacia is the Australian wattles). Thorny (African), flat crowns, insect-pollinated, pods eaten by browsers which spread the seed; giraffe and goat browse; fire-adapted.

traits.leaf_shape: compound or lobed leaves in a flat spreading crown
traits.trunk: single trunk, flat-topped crown or, for herbs, a huge single leaf on a stalk
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

bark.notes: grey to blackish-brown, deeply furrowed; young stems shiny red-brown; paired straight whitish spines with swollen bases to 6 cm

leaf.notes: bipinnate, 2-5 pairs of pinnae with 8-18 pairs of small leaflets; denser and darker green than tortilis

flower.form: bright golden-yellow ball flowers, late winter to summer

fruit.form: large thick half-moon / kidney pods to 13 x 5 cm covered in velvety grey hairs; do not split

appearance.seasonal: semi-deciduous; briefly bare in late dry season
appearance.silhouette: wide spreading rounded to flat umbrella crown on a stout dark trunk; the lone big tree of the Kalahari dunes
appearance.refs: PlantZAfrica Vachellia erioloba; Wikipedia; Kew POWO

Seeds reportedly roasted as a coffee substitute; ripening and rot times estimated.

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with two oval cotyledons, then small bipinnate leaves with only one or two pairs of pinnae and a few pairs of glossy dark green leaflets, on a zigzag stem armed with paired straight whitish spines. It branches low into a dense, rigid, very thorny little shrub whose dark bark and dark foliage give the blackbrush look early.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Vachellia rigidula): shrub 1.5-4.6 m of South Texas and NE Mexico, rich in amines and alkaloids. Germination, growth, first flowering and lifespan estimated from related Tamaulipan thornscrub acacias.

fruiting.source: Estimated from the species' usual description: fragrant creamy-white to pale yellow cylindrical flower spikes in early spring, a noted bee plant; narrow dark reddish-brown to blackish pods that split in summer. Fruit set, timings and crop estimated from related acacias.

shrub.name: Facheiro cactus
shrub.source: Pilosocereus pachycladus, facheiro, blue columnar cactus of the Brazilian Caatinga, 2-6 m — Wikipedia / LLIFLE

shrub.silhouette: blue columnar cactus, few upright arms

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are tiny pale globes with fine spines that soon elongate into a single upright, ribbed column, strikingly blue with a waxy bloom. Young stems carry dense golden to brown spines; with age it branches from low down into a candelabra of powder-blue columns, with tufts of long white wool at the flowering areoles near the tips.
growth.source: Estimated from columnar cacti of the Caatinga (Pilosocereus: nurse-plant establishment, slow early growth, branching from the base, woolly flowering areoles) and the species' description as a blue, tree-like cactus to about 10 m

fruiting.source: Estimated from Pilosocereus: nocturnal, white, tubular-bell flowers from woolly areoles visited by glossophagine bats; depressed-globose fruits that split to show magenta-purple pulp with small black seeds, eaten by birds, lizards and people

shrub.silhouette: tall spiny grey poles, leaves in rows

growth.juvenile_note: Young plants are a low, sprawling tangle of many thin, grey, spiny stems set with small round-oval fleshy leaves and conical spines in neat rows; this juvenile bush lasts several years. Then one strong central stem shoots up and becomes a tall grey spiny column that branches only high up, while the basal tangle dies off. Leafy in the wet season, bare in the dry.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Alluaudia procera: main stem to 15 m; young plants a tangle of stems for several years before a strong central stem develops; ~2.5 cm oval leaves with conical spines, deciduous in the long dry season; dioecious) and Wikipedia Didiereaceae (juvenile procumbent shrub phase). Rates, ages and first flowering estimated.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (small green-yellow unisexual flowers of four tepals clustered at the stem tops, on separate male and female plants). Flowering months, insect pollinators, the small dry one-seeded fruit and timings estimated from Didiereaceae descriptions.

shrub.name: Mandacaru
shrub.source: Cereus jamacaru, mandacaru, candelabra columnar cactus of NE Brazil Caatinga, up to 8 m — Wikipedia

growth.juvenile_note: Two small fleshy cotyledons, then a little spiny green globe that stretches into a slender 4-6 ribbed column with yellowish spines, often sheltered by a shrub. After some years it branches from low down and candelabra-like, becoming a tree-like cactus with a woody trunk.
growth.source: Wikipedia Cereus jamacaru (to 5-9 m, rarely 15 m; trunk to 45 cm; 4-6 ribs; spines to 10 cm; flowers ~30 cm, one night; fruit ~12 x 6 cm, carmine red, white pulp, seeds ~3 mm); growth rates and ages estimated from columnar cereoid cacti

fruiting.source: Wikipedia Cereus jamacaru (white nocturnal flowers ~30 cm long open at dusk, wither by morning; fruit ~12 cm long, carmine to coral red, splitting to white pulp with black seeds, eaten by people and birds); hawkmoth pollination from Caatinga cactus studies; ripening and crop estimated

shrub.name: Whistling thorn

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with two oval cotyledons and small feathery bipinnate leaves on a wiry stem armed with paired straight white spines. Saplings in the black-clay grasslands are browsed and burned back, staying spiny multi-stemmed bushes for years; then they start making swollen hollow thorn bases (bulbs, soft and green at first, hardening purple-black, then grey) that ants move into.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Vachellia drepanolobium): up to 6 m, on East African black-cotton soils, hollow swollen thorns housing Crematogaster and Tetraponera ants (C. mimosae on about half the trees). Germination, growth, first flowering and lifespan estimated from related East African savanna acacias.

shrub.source: East African black-cotton savanna; ant galls. Kew POWO (African acacias are now Vachellia/Senegalia; Acacia is the Australian wattles). Thorny (African), flat crowns, insect-pollinated, pods eaten by browsers which spread the seed; giraffe and goat browse; fire-adapted.

Flowering months, timings and crop estimated.

shrub.name: Bluewood condalia
shrub.source: Condalia hookeri, Rhamnaceae: brasil or bluewood, a dense, thorny, bright green shrub or small tree 2-6 m of the Tamaulipan thornscrub of south Texas and NE Mexico, with tiny spoon-shaped leaves and sweet black fruit — Flora of North America / Texas Native Plants Database / Kew POWO

leaf.note: small spoon-shaped bright green leaves in clusters on short spur shoots

shrub.silhouette: dense bright green thorny bush, rigid zig-zag twigs

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds sprout after summer rains, often where birds have dropped them under mesquite. The seedling is a stiff, zig-zag stem whose side twigs end in sharp spines, with tiny bright green leaves; it branches into a dense, intricately thorny, rounded bush and in time a small many-stemmed tree.
growth.source: Flora of North America Condalia hookeri (shrub or tree to 9 m, branchlets spine-tipped, leaves 0.8-2.5 cm spatulate, drupes black, sweet). Growth and ages estimated.

fruiting.source: Flora of North America Condalia hookeri (small greenish flowers in leaf axils; drupes 5-7 mm, black when ripe, juicy and sweet, eaten by birds and used for jelly). Flowering months, set and crop estimated.

bark.notes: grey bark becoming shallowly fissured; rigid zig-zag twigs ending in spines

leaf.note: small oval leaves felted with silvery-grey hairs

shrub.silhouette: rounded silver bush, lavender after rain

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds sprout on bare caliche after summer rain. The seedling is a small upright stem with felty silver leaves; it grows slowly into a dense, rounded, silver-grey bush whose whole surface flushes lavender-pink a few days after each good rain.
growth.source: Flora of North America Leucophyllum frutescens (shrub to 2.5 m; leaves silvery-tomentose; flowers bell-shaped, lavender to pink, triggered by rain and high humidity, summer-autumn). Germination, growth and lifespan estimated from horticultural data.

fruiting.source: Flora of North America Leucophyllum frutescens (solitary bell-shaped lavender-pink flowers 2-2.5 cm in leaf axils, opening in flushes after rain; small two-valved capsules). Set and crop estimated.

ground.name: Wall moss

growth.juvenile_note: Spores sprout into a green protonemal web in mortar joints and on brick or stone within weeks, soon budding tiny upright shoots. Cushions are small, dense and greyish-green, under 1 cm tall, of tongue-shaped leaves tipped with long silvery hair points that make them look hoary, and are soon topped by many upright cylindrical capsules on 0.6-1.5 cm stalks.
growth.source: Wikipedia Tortula muralis (greyish-green cushions to 1 cm tall, hair-pointed leaves, seta 0.6-1.5 cm, urn 1.5-2.7 mm, autoicous, cosmopolitan on walls, concrete, rocks and soil). Capsules are produced abundantly; spore-to-cushion time, spread and cushion age estimated from moss biology.

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.silhouette: low curly sod laced with wiry runners

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are small tufts of short, curling blades; within the first season they send out wiry, reddish stolons that root at the nodes and start new tufts, so a plant becomes a low, curly sod like buffalograss. It greens within days of rain and goes dormant tan in drought.
growth.source: Flora of North America Hilaria belangeri (stoloniferous perennial 10-30 cm, leaves 1-10 cm, flowers with summer rains); USDA NRCS plant guide (spreads by stolons, greens up quickly after rain, tolerant of grazing). Lifespan estimated.

leaf.notes: short grey-green blades that curl as they dry, in a dense low sod with wiry runners

flower.form: short spikes of clustered spikelets on slender stalks above the sod

appearance.seasonal: green after rain, tan and curled in drought
appearance.silhouette: low curly sod laced with wiry runners
appearance.refs: Flora of North America vol. 25; USDA NRCS

ground.name: Hoary grimmia

growth.juvenile_note: Spores lodge in hairline cracks on bare sunny rock and sprout into a tiny green web that buds short shoots. These grow only in the few wet days of the year, so a cushion takes years to reach a centimetre; dry for months, it sits as a whitish-grey patch on the stone and greens briefly after storms.
growth.source: Flora of North America vol. 27 and BBS field guide (cushions grey-white, leaves with long hyaline awns, on dry exposed siliceous rock, very drought-tolerant, cosmopolitan in warm dry regions). Growth and ages estimated from moss biology.

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; dries out and revives with rain, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.source: Grimmia laevigata, Grimmiaceae: compact hoary-grey cushions 1-2 cm high on exposed, sun-baked acid rock in dry climates on every continent, whitened by long hair points on every leaf; one of the most drought-hardy mosses — British Bryological Society field guide / Flora of North America vol. 27

leaf.notes: tiny broad leaves each tipped with a long white hair point, so the cushion looks frosted white-grey

appearance.seasonal: white-grey when dry, olive-green for a day after rain
appearance.refs: Flora of North America vol. 27; British Bryological Society field guide

ground.name: Rounded earthstar
ground.source: Geastrum saccatum Fr., rounded earthstar, in leaf litter of tropical and warm-temperate forest worldwide including Mesoamerican dry forest (Index Fungorum; Sunhede 1989 Geastraceae; Wikipedia)
ground.silhouette: small buff stars in the leaf litter

cap.form: brown spore sac 1-2 cm with a fringed mouth sitting in a deep saucer of 5-9 pointed rays, 2-5 cm across
cap.notes: pale buff star with a dark central puff ball; raindrops puff spores from the mouth

underside.type: none; spores puff from the apical mouth

appearance.habit: scattered in leaf litter under trees
appearance.seasonal: fruits after rain then rots (soft) or persists (woody brackets)
appearance.silhouette: small buff stars in the leaf litter
appearance.refs: Sunhede 1989 Synopsis Fungorum 1; Wikipedia Geastrum saccatum

repro.note: The mycelium is the organism and lives in the substrate for years; the mushroom is a days-long fruiting body. 'rhizome' here = the mycelium spreading through connected dead wood or litter; 'wind' = spores.

ground.name: Desert shaggy mane

repro.note: The mycelium is the organism and lives in the substrate for years; the fruiting body is what is seen. 'rhizome' here = the mycelium spreading through the substrate; 'wind' = spores.

ground.source: Podaxis pistillaris (desert shaggy mane), a secotioid fungus of sandy desert soil and termite mounds in the hot deserts of the Americas, Africa, Arabia, India and Australia; the white scaly club-shaped head never opens and fills with dark spores; the young head is eaten in parts of Arabia, Africa and Australia. Index Fungorum for the name; Wikipedia.

traits.native_range: Sandy soil of hot deserts worldwide
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

cap.form: elongated egg- to club-shaped head 5-15 cm long that never opens, white and shaggy-scaly, splitting with age to show a dark brown-black powdery spore mass
cap.notes: looks like a shaggy inkcap on a stiff stalk; turns brown and papery when old

appearance.habit: solitary or scattered on sand, often from old termite mounds
appearance.seasonal: fruits after rain; dried fruitbodies stand for months
appearance.silhouette: white shaggy clubs standing on bare sand

ground.name: Wavy scaly cloak fern
ground.origin: SW United States to South America
ground.soil_note: A rock-crevice fern: rooted in cracks and ledges of bare rock, never in loose sand or alluvium, so on wash banks it takes the rocky sides, not the sandy floor. pH any: not narrowed to one kind of rock here.

growth.juvenile_note: Spores that lodge in a shaded rock crack grow into a tiny green prothallus during wet spells; the first fronds are small and simple to few-lobed, then come short once-pinnate fronds with a few wavy pinnae. Over several wet seasons the clump builds a tuft of long, narrow, upright fronds wedged in the crack, growing only while it is wet.
growth.source: Spore-to-sporeling time, growth rate and lifespan estimated from fern biology and the genus habit (first fronds simpler than the adult's; growth only after rains); not measured for this species. Adult plant: Kew POWO; Flora of North America vol. 2.

repro.note: spores, no flowers: shed by wind from under the scale layer of fertile fronds; the prothallus grows only in wet spells, so spread reads the rains, not pollinators; compact stem, no clonal spread

ground.source: Astrolepis sinuata (Lag. ex Sw.) D.M.Benham & Windham, wavy scaly cloak fern; long known as Notholaena sinuata (Lag. ex Sw.) Kaulf. and also placed in Cheilanthes, moved to Astrolepis (the star-scaled cloak ferns) by Benham & Windham in 1992. Southwestern United States and Mexico south through Central America into South America, on rocky slopes, ledges and crevices in desert mountains, canyons and dry scrub; tufts of erect, narrow, once-pinnate fronds 20-60 cm, the pinnae shallowly wavy-lobed, grey-green with small star-shaped scales above and densely scaly beneath; the fronds curl and go dull in drought and revive after rain. Temperature, moisture and elevation bands estimated from the range and habitat, not measured. Kew POWO; Flora of North America vol. 2.

traits.native_range: Rocky slopes, ledges and crevices, SW United States to South America
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

leaf.notes: long narrow once-pinnate fronds, a ladder of many small oblong pinnae with shallow wavy lobes; upper side grey-green flecked with tiny pale star-shaped scales, underside hidden under a dense pale tan scale layer that also covers the spores

appearance.seasonal: evergreen; in drought the fronds curl and go dull, and open green again after rain
appearance.silhouette: upright tuft of narrow grey-green ladder fronds in rock cracks
appearance.refs: Kew POWO; Flora of North America vol. 2

ground.silhouette: upright tuft of narrow grey-green ladder fronds in rock cracks

desiccation.source: Astrolepis sinuata: the fronds curl and go dull in drought and revive after rain. Inferred, not measured: the scaly underside showing as the pinnae fold, and every timing - drying set slower than the epiphytic resurrection fern's (a rock crack holds water after rain), revival copied from it. The designer tunes.

ground.name: Spiny cliffbrake
ground.origin: SW United States and northern Mexico
ground.soil_note: A rock-crevice fern: rooted in cracks and ledges of bare rock, never in loose sand or alluvium, so on wash banks it takes the rocky sides, not the sandy floor. pH any: not narrowed to one kind of rock here.

growth.juvenile_note: Spores that lodge in a shaded rock crack grow into a tiny green prothallus during wet spells; the first fronds are small few-lobed blades on thin dark stalks, later ones once and then twice divided. The clump stays compact, adding a few stiff blue-green fronds in each wet season.
growth.source: Spore-to-sporeling time, growth rate and lifespan estimated from fern biology and the genus habit (first fronds simpler than the adult's; growth only after rains); not measured for this species. Adult plant: Kew POWO; Flora of North America vol. 2.

repro.note: spores, no flowers: sporangia along the segment edges under the rolled-under margins, shed by wind; the prothallus grows only in wet spells, so spread reads the rains, not pollinators; compact stem, no clonal spread

ground.source: Pellaea truncata Goodding, spiny cliffbrake: southwestern United States and northern Mexico, on rocky slopes, cliffs and crevices in desert mountains and canyons; compact clumps of stiff fronds 15-45 cm on dark brown, glossy stalks, twice divided into small, narrow, leathery, bluish-green segments with rolled-under edges, each ending in a short sharp tip. Temperature, moisture and elevation bands estimated from the range and habitat, not measured. Kew POWO; Flora of North America vol. 2.

petiole.notes: dark brown, glossy, wiry stipe and rachis
